name: OpenAPI Specification
vendor: OpenAPI Initiative (Linux Foundation), started as Swagger at Wordnik

foundation.via: SmartBear donated the Swagger Specification when the OpenAPI Initiative was announced

summary: A standard, language-neutral way to describe an HTTP API in one JSON or YAML document, from which tools generate docs, client SDKs, server stubs, tests, gateway configs and AI tools.
intro: An OpenAPI description is a JSON or YAML document that lists an API’s paths, the HTTP operations on each (`get`, `post` and so on), their parameters, request bodies and possible responses, and the security schemes that protect them. Shared data models live under `components`, written as Schema Objects. Since version 3.1 a Schema Object is JSON Schema: by default the 2020-12 draft with a few OpenAPI keywords added, so the same schemas can validate payloads elsewhere. The specification calls itself “a standard, programming language-agnostic interface description for HTTP APIs”: it says what an API accepts and returns, not how it is built or what the calls mean together.

Its value is the tooling that reads one file. Swagger UI and Redocly render reference docs; OpenAPI Generator and Microsoft’s Kiota generate client SDKs and server stubs; Spectral and Redocly CLI lint a description against a style guide; AWS API Gateway, Google API Gateway and Azure API Management import one to set up routes; and Speakeasy turns one into SDKs or an MCP server whose tools are the API’s operations. Teams either write the description first and generate code from it, or generate it from code, as FastAPI does from Python type hints. The OpenAPI Initiative also publishes two companion specifications: Arazzo, for multi-step workflows across API calls, and Overlay, for patching a description without editing its source.
strengths: One machine-readable contract drives docs, SDKs, mocks, tests, linting and gateway setup, so they stay consistent with each other
Works with any HTTP API style and any server language: it describes the HTTP surface, not the implementation
Vendor-neutral and widely supported: the three big clouds’ API gateways import it, and the main SDK, docs and linting tools read it
Schemas are JSON Schema since 3.1, so the same models can validate requests and data outside the API
Open process: anyone can join the weekly calls and propose changes, and the 3.x line has kept changes small and documented
limits: Tool support trails the specification: AWS API Gateway imports only OpenAPI 2.0 and 3.0, though 3.1 came out in 2021 and 3.2 in 2025, so check every tool in your chain before using newer features
It describes single HTTP operations, not how they fit together; call sequences need Arazzo or prose, and event-driven APIs are usually described with AsyncAPI instead
A description written by hand drifts from the code unless CI checks one against the other; one generated from code is only as good as the annotations
Flexible schemas (`oneOf`, `anyOf`, discriminators) are valid OpenAPI but hard for code generators to turn into clean types, so generated SDKs vary a lot in quality

sections.title: What each version changed
sections.intro: Each minor version can break documents written for the one before, so tools state which versions they read. Patch releases such as 3.1.2 and 3.2.1 only clarify the text.

rows.label: Swagger 2.0
values: The last version under the Swagger name; still read by most tools, and the newest that some gateways accept

rows.label: OpenAPI 3.0
values: First release under the OpenAPI name: reusable `components`, request bodies, several servers per API, links and callbacks

rows.label: OpenAPI 3.1
values: Schema Objects become JSON Schema 2020-12, with breaking changes to file uploads; webhooks; a `jsonSchemaDialect` field

rows.label: OpenAPI 3.2
values: Nested tags; the `QUERY` method and any other method; streaming media types such as server-sent events; a `querystring` parameter location

notes: OpenAPI 3.2.1, a patch release that clarifies parameter encoding, came out on September 10, 2026.
Work on a 4.0, called Moonwalk, has no planned end date; its group recommends the 3.x versions in the meantime.

sections.title: The OpenAPI Initiative’s other specifications
sections.intro: Two companion formats sit next to OpenAPI and point into OpenAPI descriptions rather than replacing them.

items.name: Arazzo
items.text: Describes sequences of API calls and the dependencies between them, such as “log in, then create an order, then pay”, in a form both people and machines can follow; its README lists generated docs, test automation and deterministic calls by AI models among the uses.

items.name: Overlay
items.text: A separate document of changes to apply to an OpenAPI description, such as translated text, per-environment settings or gateway metadata, so the source description stays untouched.

items.name: Moonwalk
items.text: A special interest group designing the next major version, which aims to describe any HTTP API, separate concerns into modules and come with an automatic upgrade from 3.x.

story: Tony Tam started Swagger in early 2010 at Wordnik, an online dictionary company, as a way to describe its API. The first Swagger Specification was released in August 2011, together with Swagger UI and a code generator, and version 2.0 followed in September 2014.

In March 2015 SmartBear Software bought the Swagger project from Reverb Technologies, Wordnik’s parent company. Eight months later, on November 5, 2015, the Linux Foundation announced the Open API Initiative with 3Scale, Apigee, Capital One, Google, IBM, Intuit, Microsoft, PayPal, Restlet and SmartBear, and SmartBear donated the specification to it. On January 1, 2016 it was renamed the OpenAPI Specification; “Swagger” stayed with SmartBear’s tools.

The first version made under the new governance, 3.0, came out in July 2017. Version 3.1 in February 2021 replaced OpenAPI’s own variant of JSON Schema with the real thing, and 3.2 in September 2025 added streaming and new HTTP methods. Since 2024 the initiative has also published Arazzo and Overlay.

choices.choice: Give the specification to a neutral foundation
choices.why: Competing API vendors were unlikely to build on a format one of them owned. At the launch, Apigee called open governance under the Linux Foundation “the necessary next step”, and Restlet said the API community should “unite around a common API language”.

choices.choice: Rename it, but let SmartBear keep “Swagger”
choices.why: Renaming separated the vendor-neutral description format from SmartBear’s Swagger tools, which kept the old name.

choices.choice: Adopt JSON Schema in 3.1, even at the cost of breaking changes
choices.why: Earlier versions used an extended subset of an old JSON Schema draft, so schemas didn’t behave the same in OpenAPI tools and JSON Schema validators. Version 3.1 moved to JSON Schema 2020-12 and accepted breaking changes to do it.
